newsitem.title: GERMANY: Rolls wants to build "socially acceptable" car.
newsitem.headline: Rolls wants to build "socially acceptable" car.

text.p: Rolls-Royce, a badge of wealth and privilege on four wheels, hopes to be a bit more politically correct with its first totally new model in nearly two decades, which is due by the turn of the century.
Rolls-Royce Motor Cars Ltd. Chief Executive Graham Morris said Thursday he wants the British automaker's new model to have "more socially acceptable shapes."
"To some people it has become an icon of a social past," Morris said of the Rolls-Royce, a work of art that embodies about as much luxury as one can expect in a car.
"Some people would say it is positive, some people negative. Obviously with the new product, we recognise that and want to move forward," Morris said in a talk with journalists.
Morris is generally tight-lipped about the new model, the first new vehicle to be introduced by the maker since 1980, when it launched the Silver Spirit.

"We have realised the fact that the products must move with the times but also maintain their link with the heritage of the Rolls-Royce and Bentley marks," Morris said of the new model, which will be offered under the Rolls-Royce and Bentley brands.
His other comment: "It will be priced competitively."
But Rolls-Royce appears to be feeling the pressure to change with the times, particularly in Western Europe where flaunting wealth has taken a back seat.
The social changes have been particularly strong in Britain, where executives with skyrocketing salaries have come under public fire and have been dubbed "fat cats."
"The British press unfortunately keeps on saying that 'fat cats' buy Rolls-Royces. That is not true," Morris said.
"The heads of major corporations who used to drive our cars can no longer do so because shareholders demand that they lower their vision and be a little bit more prudent," he said.
Instead, Morris said Rolls-Royce's customers are often businessmen in their 50s who own their own cars or people who have inherited wealth and spend their money as they like.
"We are tending to find that our buyers are owners of a business or major shareholders of a business, both medium- and small-sized, that have been successful, worked hard," he said.
"We still obviously get people who, through family or history, have acquired wealth," Morris said.
But Rolls is searching for fresh buyers to fulfil Morris' goal of raising sales by about 50 percent from the 1996 level of 1,744 cars in the coming years, in part with the help of the new model.
The company is owned by engineering group Vickers Plc and is no longer connected to airplane engine manufacturer Rolls-Royce Plc.
One step has been to revamp the carmaker's dealer network by paring down the number of locations and making them more exclusive.
"We are not really a car dealer, we are in the luxury goods segment," Morris said, comparing Rolls-Royce to a pricey tailor who can make a product fit the needs of individual customers.
The new dealerships will have salons where customers can build their own Rolls-Royce or Bentley from scratch from a dizzying array of options, or even create some of their own.

"About 50 percent of the cars we now sell are individualized," Morris said. "It is our desire that in the future this would rise to 100 percent and the layout of our new dealerships is a hope to do just that."
